bugOrRegression.description: Reduced the 5s delay before tainting `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute` when a Node became unreachable.
bugOrRegression.author: tnqn
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Reduce 5s delay of tainting `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute` when a Node becomes unreachable

issueContext.title: NoExecute taint is added with extra 5s delay when a Node's ready condition becomes Unknown
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When investigating a delay of Pod eviction on unreachable Node, I found it always took 5s longer than the desired duration.
Looking at the timestamps, I found an odd one: the timestamp when `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` NoExecute taint was added.

```
# Node taints:
taints:
- effect: NoSchedule
  key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
  timeAdded: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
- effect: NoExecute
  key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
  timeAdded: "2023-09-21T06:32:46Z"    # This one is 5s later than all other timestamps

# Node conditions:
conditions:
- lastHeartbeatTime: "2023-09-21T06:31:55Z"
  lastTransitionTime: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
  message: Kubelet stopped posting node status.
  reason: NodeStatusUnknown
  status: Unknown
  type: MemoryPressure
- lastHeartbeatTime: "2023-09-21T06:31:55Z"
  lastTransitionTime: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
  message: Kubelet stopped posting node status.
  reason: NodeStatusUnknown
  status: Unknown
  type: DiskPressure
- lastHeartbeatTime: "2023-09-21T06:31:55Z"
  lastTransitionTime: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
  message: Kubelet stopped posting node status.
  reason: NodeStatusUnknown
  status: Unknown
  type: PIDPressure
- lastHeartbeatTime: "2023-09-21T06:31:55Z"
  lastTransitionTime: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
  message: Kubelet stopped posting node status.
  reason: NodeStatusUnknown
  status: Unknown
  type: Ready

# Pod conditions:
- lastProbeTime: null
  lastTransitionTime: "2023-09-21T06:32:41Z"
  status: "False"
  type: Ready
```

This can be reproducd consistently by terminating kubelet on a Node. The 5s delay of tainting adds 5s delay to the recovery time of Pods which are supposed to be evicted by the taint and recreated on other Nodes sooner. And I can't think of a reason why this taint alone should be added 5s later after the other taint and all other status changes. After investigating the relevant code for how the 5s is introduced, I think it should be an unwante

enrichment.problem: When a node's Ready condition turns Unknown, the NoExecute taint `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` is added 5 seconds after the NoSchedule taint, causing pods to be evicted later than the intended time.
enrichment.affected: Pods running on nodes that become unreachable; cluster operators monitoring node health and pod eviction.
enrichment.fix: The extra 5‑second delay is removed, so the NoExecute taint is applied immediately when the node becomes unreachable, aligning it with the NoSchedule taint timestamp.
enrichment.impact: Pods on a node that becomes unreachable are evicted promptly, reducing the window where dead pods linger and improving workload reliability and cluster health.

bugOrRegression.description: The `baseline` and `restricted` pod security admission levels blocked setting the `host` field on probe and lifecycle handlers.
bugOrRegression.author: tssurya
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: The `baseline` and `restricted` pod security admission levels now block setting the `host` field on probe and lifecycle handlers

issueContext.title: Pod probes lead to blind SSRF from the node
issueContext.body:
Note: I disclosed this private and was asked to open in public

#### What happened:

A pod probe can be configured to send readiness probes to arbitrary destinations, including localhost on the node. This is similar to CVE-2020-8555.

Kubernetes Version:
v0.20.0 (Kind) and v1.19.6 (GKE) were tested. I suspect its an issue on all versions

Steps To Reproduce:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - image: docker.io/kennethreitz/httpbin
    name: httpbin
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        host: 169.254.169.254
        httpHeaders:
        - name: Metadata-Flavor
          value: Google
        path: /computeMetadata/v1/
        port: 80
        scheme: HTTP
```

This shows an example of accessing GCE metadata.

Other possible targets are localhost endpoints, such as 127.0.0.1:2381/metrics (etcd metrics), or external targets (httpbin.org, for example).

Note that because this is coming from the node, we can also access internal targets (pods) running on the same node, **bypassing NetworkPolicy restrictions**.

In generally, the attack only allows sending GET requests, and does not allow viewing the data in the response.

The status code of a response is, however, returned in pod events: "HTTP probe failed with statuscode: .... This could be used to extract some degree of private information about the node.

Additionally, access to kubelet logs with verbosity >= 4 will log the full body, which would make this much work severe.

Other possible risks are that these external calls are now coming from the k8s node which may have differing firewall/routing rules than a pod would.

#### What you expected to happen:

I don't know. Its certainly a tricky problem since its a part of the API and hard to change.

enrichment.problem: Baseline and restricted Pod Security Admission levels allowed the `host` field to be set on probe and lifecycle handlers, enabling pods to perform blind SSRF requests from the node (e.g., to metadata services) and bypass NetworkPolicy restrictions.
enrichment.affected: All pods validated under the `baseline` or `restricted` Pod Security Admission levels; clusters that enable these PSA profiles.
enrichment.fix: The admission controller now rejects pods that set the `host` field on any probe (readiness/liveness/startup) or lifecycle handler when the cluster is using the `baseline` or `restricted` PSA levels.
enrichment.impact: Prevents pods from reaching arbitrary network endpoints via host‑based probes, protecting node metadata, internal services, and respecting NetworkPolicy. Enhances cluster security for all workloads under the stricter PSA profiles.

issueContext.title: Job controller's race condition - Pod finalizer removal and job uncounted status update should work in separate reconcile
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Job controller accidentally created two pods even if the Job spec specifies in a busy cluster:

```
  parallelism: 1
  completions: 1
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 86400
  backoffLimit: 0
```

This is happening because when job controller is calculating the succeed pods, it's taking three inputs ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L892)):

1. The completion count from `Job.status.succeeded`
2. The existing succeed pods (if the finalizer is still present)
3. The uncounted completion count from `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods`

Due to the current implementation where the job controller is refreshing both (2) and (3) in the same reconcile/sync process:

> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1165-L1167

The job controller may miscount the succeeded pods when the watch event for (3) hasn't reach the controller. A delayed watch event is fairly likely to happened in a busy cluster.

### What did you expect to happen?

The better implementation should be handling the refreshing of (2) and (3) in separate reconcile process:

(1) in the 1st reconcile, job controller should only refresh `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods` while preserving the finalizers on the pods
(2) in the 2nd reconcile which is triggered by (1), job controller is safe to remove the finalizers from pods

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Any trivial job with 1 completion on a busy cluster should be able to reproduce the issue

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

All k8s versions I assume

### Cloud provider

Any

### OS version

Any

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

enrichment.problem: The Job controller could miscount succeeded pods due to handling of finalizers and uncounted terminated pods in the same reconcile loop, leading to creation of extra Pods for Jobs that are already marked finished (successful or failed).
enrichment.affected: Users running Job workloads, especially those with low parallelism/completions and in busy clusters where watch events may be delayed.
enrichment.fix: The controller now separates the refresh of `Job.status.uncountedTerminatedPods` and the removal of pod finalizers into separate reconciliation passes, preventing the miscount and eliminating the creation of unnecessary Pods.
enrichment.impact: Prevents wasteful creation of Pods for completed Jobs, conserving cluster resources and ensuring Job completion semantics are respected.

issueContext.title: Parallel pod management with maxUnavailable set should not ignore minReadySeconds
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

StatefulSet spec's template was updated:

<details>

```apiVersion: v1
items:
- apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: StatefulSet
  # many other unrelated stuff
  spec:
    replicas: 5
    minReadySeconds: 300
    podManagementPolicy: Parallel
    updateStrategy:
      rollingUpdate:
        maxUnavailable: 1
```
</details>

`status.availableReplicas` has dropped from 5 to 0 over the course of the push (which took ≈3 minutes).

### What did you expect to happen?

`status.availableReplicas` should not have been dropped below 4 at any point (as `maxUnavailable` is explicitly set to 1).

Create a `StatefulSet` with the spec above, and update its `spec.template` field to trigger a rollout.

issueContext.title: Statefulset with podManagementPolicy=Parallel ignores minReadySeconds on statefulset rollout update
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Deployed a statefulset with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` and with `minReadySeconds: 15`, have waited for all the pods being ready. Then, issued a rollout restart on the sts.

### What did you expect to happen?

Expected that the rollout update happens the same way as with `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady`, that is the last pod is terminated, then restarted, waited to be ready, and then waiting for the extra `minReadySeconds` to pass before moving the next pod. Instead, once the pod became ready, the rollout process instantly moved to the next pod, ignoring the `minReadySeconds` setting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply the following sts:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  minReadySeconds: 10
  podManagementPolicy: Parallel
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      application: web
  serviceName: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        application: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: web
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
```

Wait until all pods become ready. Then, issue a rollout restart:

```
$ kubectl rollout restart sts web
```

Then, observe that as soon a pod enters ready state, the upgrade process moves to the next pod, ignoring `minReadySeconds` value.

If the sts is created with default `podManagementPolicy`, the update procedure works as expected.


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"27", GitVersion:"v1.27.3", GitCommit:"25b4e43193bcda6c7328a6d147b1fb73a33f1598", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2023-06-14T09:53:42Z", GoVersion:"go1.20.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Kustomize Version: v5.0.1
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"27", GitVersion:"v1.27.3", GitCommit:"25b4e43193bcda6c7328

enrichment.problem: StatefulSet controller ignored `minReadySeconds` when using `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` (and during scale‑down with OrderedReady). Pods were considered ready immediately after passing readiness probes, causing rollouts or scaling to proceed without the configured wait time, which could drop available replicas below the intended `maxUnavailable` guarantee.

Upon pod restart, the NodeExpandVolume operation successfully resizes the file system.

issueContext.title: NodeResizeError persists after successful PVC resize with CSI drivers lacking NodeExpandVolume support
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

After resizing a PVC backed by the CephFS CSI driver (which does not implement NodeExpandVolume), Kubernetes successfully performs the controller-side resize. The PVC's capacity and allocatedResources fields are updated to the correct value, and the volume is usable in the pod.

However, the PVC status remains in a NodeResizeError condition indefinitely, with a message like:

```
conditions:
- type: NodeResizeError
  status: "True"
  message: failed to expand pvc with NodeExpand is not supported by the CSI driver rook-ceph.cephfs.csi.ceph.com

```
This happens even after pod restarts and with RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure=true enabled. The error condition is cosmetic — the filesystem is resized correctly — but it is never cleared, causing persistent alerts and misleading status.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes (or the external resizer) should detect that:

*    The CSI driver does not support NodeExpandVolume

*    The resize succeeded on the controller side

*    The PVC is healthy and matches the requested size

It should then automatically clear the NodeResizeError condition.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.    Use the Rook CephFS CSI driver with a StorageClass that allows volume expansion.

2.    Ensure the CSI driver supports ControllerExpandVolume but not NodeExpandVolume.

3.    Enable RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure=true on the kube-controller-manager.

4.    Create and bind a PVC.

5.    Resize the PVC by increasing its spec.resources.requests.storage.

 6.   Wait for pod to restart or manually restart the pod.

7.    Observe that the PVC is resized (capacity and allocatedResources match), but NodeResizeError condition is never cleared.


### Anything else we need to know?

This is not a functional error — the PVC works as intended. However, the error condition misleads monitoring tools and operators. It appears that Kubernetes never recovers from a permanent NodeExpandVolume failur

enrichment.problem: When a CSI driver supports controller-side volume expansion but does not implement NodeExpandVolume, PVCs with the ReadWriteMany access mode were left with a persistent NodeResizeError condition in their status, even though the resize succeeded. This false error caused misleading alerts and confusing status for users.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using CSI drivers that support ControllerExpandVolume but not NodeExpandVolume, with PVCs that have the ReadWriteMany access mode. The false NodeResizeError condition affected monitoring and troubleshooting workflows.
enrichment.fix: The kubelet was updated to detect that the CSI driver lacks node expansion support and, after a successful controller‑side resize, automatically clear the NodeResizeError condition from the PVC status.
enrichment.impact: Users of CSI drivers that lack node expansion (e.g., CephFS) no longer see spurious NodeResizeError conditions after a successful PVC resize. This improves observability, prevents unnecessary alert noise, and reflects the true health of the PVC.

issueContext.title: spec.jobTemplate.spec.podFailurePolicy.rules[0].onPodConditions[0].status: Required value: valid values: ["False" "True" "Unknown"]
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When I try to apply (patching) an existing `CronJob` with the following `podFailurePolicy`:
```
      podFailurePolicy:
        rules:
        - action: Ignore
          onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
```

I'm getting the following Error:
```
error when patching "/dev/shm/2794561279": CronJob.batch "mycronjob" is invalid: spec.jobTemplate.spec.podFailurePolicy.rules[0].onPodConditions[0].status: Required value: valid values: ["False" "True" "Unknown"]
```


Following the docs ([link1](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/19/kubernetes-1-31-pod-failure-policy-for-jobs-goes-ga/), [link2](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/19/kubernetes-1-31-pod-failure-policy-for-jobs-goes-ga/)), it seems to be optional.

same in code(?)

https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/c5439348b1cf0e96c7446a1bef9475553530f12f/batch/v1/types.go#L214


### What did you expect to happen?

should be applied without any errors

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

create a sample cronjob with these configurations: 

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: mycronjob
  labels:
    app: release-name
    app.kubernetes.io/name: "release-name"
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: "release-name"
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: mycronjob
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  suspend: false
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 100
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 2
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 172800 
      backoffLimit: 2
      parallelism: 1
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800
      podFailurePolicy:
        rules:
        - action: Ignore
          onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
...
```

### Anything else we need to know?

workaround: adding the field `status: 'True'` fix it

```
    podFailurePolicy:
      rules:
      - action: Ignore
        onPodConditions:
        - type: DisruptionTarget
          status: 'True'
```

issueContext.title: `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` isn't accurately respected after SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ feature
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Let's say you specify `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, you would expect the backoff is disabled completely.
However, actually the pods could experience a backoff penalty for ~0.999 seconds.

It's caused by:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a3097010faac734fb4956dbc91ae9034d0a9f840/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/backoff_queue.go#L211-L212

So, it regards the pod is backing off if `backoffTime == Truncate(now)`.
And, if you specify `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, backoffTime would always be `pInfo.Timestamp`, which is when the pod came back to the queue. Meaning, pods is regarded as backing off until ~1 second has passed after the pod came back to the queue because of `Truncate(now)`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` should be respected as an actual upper limit.
I guess if `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` is set to non-zero value, users notice this problem less likely. 
But, if it's set to 0, users could notice/be confused because they expect no backoff at all, but logs/metrics would show some pods have experienced backoff.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Set `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, put a pod in the queue via `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` (simulating the pod is unschedulable and coming back to the queue), immediately trigger some events that trigger the pod's requeueing, and see logs. 
You should see the pod is going through backoffQ.

### Anything else we need to know?

issueContext.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reporting FailedRescale error
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

We are currently running several applications that are configured with metric-based scaling. These applications are expected to scale frequently in response to varying traffic patterns.

Occasionally, we observe the following error during scaling events (though it is not frequent), and there is no noticeable impact on the actual scaling process:

```
reason: FailedRescale, New size: <size>; reason: All metrics <below>/<above> target; error: Operation cannot be fulfilled on deployments.apps: the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again.
```

Our understanding is that this occurs due to a race condition where another controller or a CI/CD process is simultaneously patching or updating the Deployment object at the same time the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) attempts to scale it.

**In some cases, we observed the issue occurring even when there were no apparent changes to the Deployment object itself. Only a possible update to the resourceVersion, which we were unable to confirm the reason for the same**


To be cautious, we have set up an alert to notify us if the HPA fails to scale a deployment for any reason. However, encountering this specific error results in unnecessary noise and false positives in our alerting system.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expect the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to perform retries internally and suppress the reporting of this error, as its occurrence generates unnecessary noise and may cause undue concern regarding system scaling.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce the issue:

- Configure a Deployment and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with CPU or memory-based scaling.
- Apply load to the Deployment pods to trigger scaling by the HPA.
- Simultaneously, perform multiple consecutive patch operations on the Deployment.

This sequence will result in the HPA reporting the same error in its events.

### Anything e

enrichment.problem: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler emitted a FailedRescale event when a scale operation initially failed due to a resource version conflict, even though the controller successfully retried and completed the scaling. This generated unnecessary alert noise.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to scale Deployments (or other scalable resources) could see misleading FailedRescale events during conflict retries.
enrichment.fix: The HPA controller now suppresses the FailedRescale event if the scale succeeds after an internal retry and instead emits a SuccessfulRescale event. A FailedRescale event is only emitted when all retries are exhausted.
enrichment.impact: Operators see accurate scaling events, reducing false‑positive alerts and improving observability of autoscaling actions. No change in scaling behavior; only event reporting is corrected.

The docs that describes PodResourceAPI are not refer explicitly to whether `List()` should ignore terminal pod's resources or not, meaning it might not be a bug at all.

enrichment.problem: Deployments with `minReadySeconds` could stall during a rollout when a pod restarts before the minimum ready period. The controller delayed updating `.status.availableReplicas`, causing the rollout to exceed progress deadlines and appear stuck.
enrichment.affected: Users running Deployments (or ReplicaSets) that specify `minReadySeconds` and perform rollouts, especially when pods may restart during the rollout.
enrichment.fix: ReplicaSets and Deployments now update `.status.availableReplicas` immediately at the correct point in the reconciliation loop, eliminating the delay. This enables faster condition updates and prevents rollouts from being blocked.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed misleading response codes in admission control metrics.
bugOrRegression.author: gavinkflam

issueContext.title: Apiserver admission control (validating, mutating webhooks) return misleading response code 400 on network errors
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When the apiserver calls a webhook, be it validating or mutating, and the configured endpoint is not reachable due to network issue (timeout, EOF due to a broken connection, rejected new connection, ...) the error defaults to a `400 Bad Request`:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9d2fc46556af162ff42a4773349d0f92f9ef8d50/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/validating/dispatcher.go#L309
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9d2fc46556af162ff42a4773349d0f92f9ef8d50/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/mutating/dispatcher.go#L308

I noticed this when analyzing some random webhook invocation errors and seeing that that the increasing `apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count` metric (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/) had `rejection_code="400"`. This metric was introduced by @roycaihw in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/81399 to expose the various causes for rejects.

With 4xx being "user side errors" and 5xx being server side errors, this mapping is clearly misleading or even incorrect and I suspected the actual webhook endpoint had responded with a 400.

But the client is clearly NOT at fault here. The 4xx even would indicate that a retry is likely not successful.




### What did you expect to happen?

Non HTTP errors from a failed connection to the webhook endpoint should be mapped to `503 Service Unavailable` with either https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/e25aab096bf1a9b677c0e04efd3870b396494782/pkg/api/errors/errors.go#L339 or even https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/e25aab096bf1a9b677c0e04efd3870b396494782/pkg/api/errors/errors.go#L386 clearly indicating that this is an internal error.

Looking at the handling of response parsing errors in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9d2fc46556af162ff42a4773349d0f92f9ef8d50/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/validating/dispatcher.go#

enrichment.problem: When a validating or mutating admission webhook endpoint is unreachable due to network issues, the apiserver incorrectly records the failure as HTTP 400 Bad Request, causing the apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count metric to show rejection_code="400". This misleads users into thinking the client request was malformed rather than a server-side connectivity problem.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use validating or mutating admission webhooks and monitor apiserver admission webhook metrics. Operators interpreting rejection_code may have misdiagnosed webhook connectivity problems.
enrichment.fix: Non-HTTP network errors from webhook calls are now mapped to HTTP 503 Service Unavailable, and the corresponding admission webhook metrics emit rejection_code="503" instead of "400".
enrichment.impact: Metrics accurately reflect server-side failures, enabling correct alerting, debugging, and retry decisions for clusters using admission webhooks.

issueContext.title: Consistent paginated lists unnecessarily falling back to etcd in 1.33
issueContext.body:
### What happened?


**When Paginated LIST calls with  rv="" and LIMIT=<x> and without continue token set, those are falling back to etcd instead of serving from cache in `1.33`**

#### TL;DR 

Issue is in Step 7 .5 below - Basically we shouldn't be returning `errors.NewResourceExpired` when snapshot is nil - [xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/544e7a63e2cb6646d19e6a17bd665b07f39843d1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L547-L548)

There is a performance impact angle to this bug - We do consistent reads to etcd with `LIMIT=1` in step 4 below, which wait until cache catches up to the RV or times out, but all of that is unnecessary cpu cycles spent on request because we are falling back to etcd (step 8) anyway, which in this case from below audit log for this specific request, it spent `721ms` unnecessarily iiuc.



### In 1.33  here the is the code flow for LIST request FMU :


1. Delegator decides if call needs to be served from cache or if it needs to be sent to etcd - [xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f20adaecd4743b3481af4240ed034003dacf7c9c/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator.go#L183) 
2. Given RV=“” in this case, it will call ShouldDelegateConsistentRead -   [xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3fb9ee0a51b6a6ea135d991391c35806422c19/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator/interface.go#L58)
3. Given consistentReads are enabled, this yields `{ ShouldDelegate : False , ConsistentRead : true}`  - [xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3fb9ee0a51b6a6ea135d991391c35806422c19/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator/interface.go#L101) 
4. Given shouldDelegate is False and ConsistentRead is true from 3 , it makes the call to etcd to get current RV -[xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3fb9ee0a51b6a6ea135d991391c35806422c19/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator.go#L210-L211)
5. Now

enrichment.problem: In Kubernetes 1.33, paginated LIST API calls with an empty resource version, a LIMIT, and no continue token incorrectly fell back to reading directly from etcd instead of being served from the watch cache. This caused unnecessary etcd load and increased request latency (e.g., ~721 ms per request).
enrichment.affected: Clients performing paginated LIST calls (e.g., `kubectl get pods --limit=...`) and any workloads that rely on fast list operations.
enrichment.fix: The regression was fixed by correcting the delegator logic so that such LIST requests are served from the cache when appropriate, preventing the fallback to etcd.

issueContext.title: kube-proxy: externalTrafficPolicy:Local and proxy-mode=nftables blackholes pods traffic to external IPs
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When using kube-proxy on nftables mode and specify a `LoadBalancer` Service with `externalTrafficPolicy:Local` that has an ExternalIP assigned, kube-proxy will create an entry in the kube-proxy ip nftable that will drop traffic to that external IP, like:

```
        map no-endpoint-services {
                type ipv4_addr . inet_proto . inet_service : verdict
                comment "vmap to drop or reject packets to services with no endpoints"
                elements = { 
                             10.88.1.2 . tcp . 80 comment "sys-ingress-priv/internal-ingress-controller-v2:web" : drop,
```

As a result, any pod on the host cannot send traffic to the external IP of the LoadBalancer.

### What did you expect to happen?

On nodes where no workload is present, traffic should not be dropped but load balanced by kube proxy to the target Service endpoints.
This will also bring consistency with how other modes work, as this issue was addressed both for ipvs (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93456)
and iptables (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/77523) modes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run kube-proxy on nftables mode and try hitting a `LoadBalancer` Service `ExternalIP` from within a pod running in a node that does not have ready endpoints of the target service

### Anything else we need to know?

@kubernetes/sig-network-bugs
Simmilar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/75262 but for `nftables` mode

issueContext.title: Custom resource objects can be created during CRD Termination using server-side apply
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

After a CRD DELETE, while the CRD finalizer is deleting all custom resource objects of that type, and the `Terminating=True` status condition is set, it should not be possible to create objects of that type, but it is with server-side apply, because the creation prevention implementation blocks by method type and there's no check in the PATCH handler.

- CREATE is blocked: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go#L373
- PATCH is not blocked: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go#L390

In the Patch Apply handler, the `forceAllowCreate` flag is set to `true`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/patch.go#L646 This allows patching to always create objects.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the CRD is terminating, SSA should not be able to create new objects.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. apply a CRD
2. apply a CR with a manual finalizer to block CRD termination
3. delete the CRD
4. create a new CR with SSA

### Anything else we need to know?

There is another race condition allowing creation, but it's otherwise unrelated to this bug, which is not a race condition: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/99181

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.28.2
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.27.4-gke.900
```

</details>

enrichment.fix: Added a termination check to the PATCH (server‑side apply) handler so that when a CRD has the `Terminating=True` condition, creation via SSA is rejected, aligning its behavior with the CREATE path.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed the problem of validation error when specifying resource requirements at the container level for a resource not supported at the pod level. It implicitly interpreted the pod-level value as 0.
bugOrRegression.author: chao-liang

issueContext.title: [Pod Level Resources] Pod-level resource validation fails when container-level is set for other resource
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When a Kubernetes Pod defines resources.requests at the Pod level, but only specifies a subset of the supported resources requested by its containers (e.g., only cpu at the Pod level, while a container requests memory), Kubernetes' validation implicitly assigns a request of "0" for the unstated resource (e.g., memory) at the Pod level. This "0" value then triggers a validation error because it's less than the actual aggregated request from the containers, even though the user might expect the Pod to implicitly aggregate the container's memory request.

```
 "pod" is invalid: spec.resources.requests[memory]: Invalid value: "0": must be greater than or equal to aggregate container requests of 10Mi
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When a user defines resource requests at the container level, Kubernetes already aggregates these requests internally to determine the total resource needs of the Pod. If the Pod.spec.resources.requests field is present, but only specifies a subset of resources (e.g., cpu but not memory), the intuitive expectation is that Kubernetes would implicitly aggregate the memory request from the containers, rather than defaulting the Pod's memory request to 0.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ccf291b50166ce82204486aae6a626a30b469182/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L4406 needs to be fixed to compare container aggregates with pod-level values only if pod-level value for that resource is set.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Enable PodLevelResources feature gate on apiserver, scheduler and kubelet, and create the following pod
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-bug
spec:
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "300m"  # Pod-level CPU request
  containers:
  - name: sleep-infinity
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
    resources:
      requests:
        ephemeral-memory: 10Mi 
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No respo

enrichment.problem: When a Pod defines resources.requests at the pod level for only a subset of resources (e.g., CPU) while a container requests another resource (e.g., memory), the missing pod-level resource is treated as 0. This causes a validation error because the pod-level request is less than the aggregated container request.
enrichment.affected: Users who set pod-level resource requests partially, causing pod creation to fail due to validation errors.
enrichment.fix: Updated the pod spec validation logic to compare aggregate container resource requests with pod-level values only when the pod-level value for that resource is explicitly set, preventing the implicit 0 interpretation.
enrichment.impact: Users can now create Pods that specify resource requests at the container level without needing to repeat every resource at the pod level, eliminating unexpected validation failures and simplifying resource specifications.

issueContext.title: Garbage collector deletes DaemonSet after updating ownerReference and deleting previous owner
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

In rare cases, I'm seeing the GC deleting a DaemonSet with a valid ownerReference. This issue looks like a time-of-check/time-of-use error in the garbage collector, although I'm unsure from the docs what behavior to expect.

I'm using a tool similar to `kubectl apply --prune`, called `synk`, except instead of using a label selector to prune old resources, it uses the Kubernetes garbage collector. However, I've found that some systems (single-node test clusters on VMs) break after a reboot, due to unexpected deletion of a DaemonSet. Strangely, I've not seen any other resources getting deleted (even DaemonSets in other manifests installed the same way), so I'm not sure what's special about this DaemonSet.

The order of events, when using this to install a manifest for kube-proxy, is as follows:

- setup (working as intended)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v1
  - synk creates the resources in the manifest, including the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet
- update (not always working)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v2
  - synk patches the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet to update its ownerReference to point to kube-proxy.v1
  - synk deletes the old owner, kube-proxy.v1
  - sometimes, the garbage collector deletes the DaemonSet, even though it still has a valid ownerReference

### What did you expect to happen?

The garbage collector should only delete resources with dangling ownerReferences. Alternatively, if it's impossible to handle the case of updated ownerReferences in general, the [GC docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/) should tell you how to update the ownerReference and wait for the GC to become aware of this, before deleting the obsolete owner (eg can the GC enforce some ceiling on the time between fetching the ownerReferences and checking them for existence?).



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely

enrichment.problem: The garbage collection controller could race with concurrent updates to an object's ownerReferences, causing it to mistakenly delete resources (e.g., DaemonSets) that still had a valid owner, leading to unexpected data loss.
enrichment.affected: Any workload that relies on ownerReferences for garbage collection, especially DaemonSet, Deployment, StatefulSet, etc., and users employing `apply --prune`‑style workflows.
enrichment.fix: Garbage collection now synchronizes with ownerReference changes when deleting orphaned objects, eliminating the time‑of‑check/time‑of‑use race and ensuring only truly orphaned resources are removed.
enrichment.impact: Prevents accidental deletion of workloads when their owning resources are updated, making tools that rely on the GC (such as `kubectl apply --prune` or custom controllers) safe and reliable.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed e2e test "[Driver: csi-hostpath] [Testpattern: Dynamic PV (filesystem volmode)] volumeLimits should support volume limits" not to leak Pods and namespaces.
bugOrRegression.author: jsafrane
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fixed e2e test "[Driver: csi-hostpath] [Testpattern: Dynamic PV (filesystem volmode)] volumeLimits should support volume limits]" not to leak Pods and namespaces.

enrichment.problem: The e2e test "[Driver: csi-hostpath] [Testpattern: Dynamic PV (filesystem volmode)] volumeLimits should support volume limits" leaked Pods and namespaces, leaving leftover resources after test execution.
enrichment.affected: Developers and CI systems running the CSI hostpath e2e tests; any workflow that relied on the affected test could encounter leaked resources.
enrichment.fix: The test logic was updated to ensure created Pods and namespaces are properly cleaned up after the test completes, preventing resource leaks.

bugOrRegression.description: DRA drivers: the resource slice controller sometimes didn't react properly when kubelet or someone else deleted a recently created ResourceSlice. It incorrectly assumed that the ResourceSlice still exists and didn't recreate it.
bugOrRegression.author: pohly

enrichment.problem: The DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation) resource slice controller sometimes failed to react when a ResourceSlice was deleted (by kubelet or other actors). It incorrectly assumed the slice still existed and therefore did not recreate it.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that enable DRA drivers and workloads that request resources provided via ResourceSlice. Pods that rely on those resources could have been impacted.
enrichment.fix: The controller now correctly checks for the existence of a ResourceSlice after a delete event and recreates the slice if it is missing, ensuring the expected resource allocation flow resumes.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed an issue where the kubelet token cache returned stale tokens when service accounts were recreated with the same name. The cache is now UID-aware. Additionally, the new `TokenRequestServiceAccountUIDValidation` feature gate (Beta, enabled by default) ensures the `TokenRequest` UID matches the service account UID when set.

issueContext.title: Token manager cache returns stale tokens when service accounts are recreated with same name
issueContext.body:
pre-existing, but getServiceAccountToken and the kubelet functions that manage / cache tokens are not aware of service account uid or the need to regenerate a token because the service account was recreated

file a separate issue for resolving this... that could involve making getServiceAccountToken optionally take the uid of the service account if known (it is known from this call site, it is not known when getting tokens for volumes), returning the service account uid in TokenRequest responses, and making the kubelet token cache smarter about invalidating if the uid is provided and doesn't match

_Originally posted by @liggitt in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132617#discussion_r2183297324_

/triage accepted
/kind bug
/sig auth
/assign

enrichment.problem: The kubelet's token cache did not consider the ServiceAccount UID, so when a ServiceAccount was deleted and recreated with the same name, the cache could serve a stale token from the previous instance.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where ServiceAccounts are deleted and recreated (e.g., CI pipelines, automated SA rotation) and workloads that consume service account tokens via the kubelet.
enrichment.fix: The token cache is now UID‑aware, invalidating entries when the UID does not match. A new beta feature gate, TokenRequestServiceAccountUIDValidation (enabled by default), adds validation that a TokenRequest’s UID, when set, matches the ServiceAccount’s UID.
enrichment.impact: Pods that rely on projected service account tokens or volume token mounts will always receive a current token after a ServiceAccount is recreated, preventing potential authentication failures or security issues caused by using outdated tokens.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed runtime cost estimation for `x-int-or-string` custom resource schemas with maximum lengths.

bugOrRegression.description: Pods were not allowed to mix the usage of `user-namespaces` (`hostUsers: false`) and `volumeDevices`. Kubernetes returned an error in this case.

bugOrRegression.description: Added validation to reject Pods using the `PodLevelResources` feature on Windows OS due to lack of support. bugOrRegression.description: DRA driver helper: Fixed handling of apiserver restart when running on a Kubernetes version which did not support the `resource.k8s.io` version used by the DRA driver.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed a bug that the async preemption feature keeps preemptor pods unnecessarily in the queue.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed prerelease lifecycle for `PodCertificateRequest`.

other.description: Removed the deprecated `--register-schedulable` command line argument from the kubelet.
other.author: carlory

other.description: Promoted the `SeparateTaintEvictionController` feature gate to GA; it is now enabled unconditionally.
other.author: carlory

enrichment.fix: The feature gate has been promoted to GA and is now enabled unconditionally, making the SeparateTaintEvictionController always active.
enrichment.impact: All clusters now get consistent, automatic handling of taint‑based pod eviction without extra configuration, improving pod placement reliability and reducing operational steps.

other.description: Added a warning to `kubectl attach`, notifying / reminding users that commands and output are available via the `log` subresource of that Pod.
other.author: mochizuki875

issueContext.title: Commands and output are logged when attached to a container via kubectl
issueContext.body:
When attached to a container, all commands and output executed during an attached session will be visible via pods/log that could be scraped.

**Repro steps:**
Run a pod and directly attach to its shell with the following command:
> kubectl run -it my-pod —image=busybox — sh

Once the pod is started and attached, anything that is typed in the terminal is not only visible in the Kubernetes console (for example in Openshift pod logs tab), but also scraped by the log-scrapers like fluentbit and are forwarded to ELK/EFK/etc.
Many SREs, infra engineers, troubleshooters run pods like this to troubleshoot and spot problems, and many times credentials and other sensitive information is used during troubleshooting. 

e.g.
> curl -u username:mypass http://example.com/ 
will log username and password on the console and eventually into logs

**Note**: when exec into a container, that session is never logged

**Proposal:**
Add a warning to remind users that `all commands and output executed when attached to a container will be visible via pods/log` to help users who might not expect this behavior

Initially reported by @yosuf

enrichment.problem: Users attaching to a container with `kubectl attach` may not realize that all commands and output are written to the pod's log subresource, which can be scraped and expose sensitive information.
enrichment.affected: Operators who use `kubectl attach` to troubleshoot pods, especially when entering credentials or sensitive data during the session.
enrichment.fix: The `kubectl attach` command now prints a warning reminding users that the session's commands and output will be logged in `pods/<name>/log`.
enrichment.impact: Improves security awareness for operators and SREs who use `kubectl attach` for troubleshooting, helping prevent accidental leakage of credentials or other sensitive data into log aggregation pipelines.

other.description: Updated `kube-controller-manager` events to support contextual logging.
other.author: mengjiao-liu
other.userFacingChange: kube-controller-manager events to support contextual logging.

enrichment.problem: Events emitted by kube‑controller‑manager did not include contextual information, making it difficult for operators to correlate controller actions with log entries and to troubleshoot issues.
enrichment.affected: Cluster administrators and operators who rely on controller‑manager events for troubleshooting and monitoring.
enrichment.fix: The kube‑controller‑manager now emits events with contextual logging support, attaching relevant request and object metadata to each event.
enrichment.impact: Improves observability and debugging of controller‑manager activity, allowing users to more easily trace actions and diagnose problems in their clusters.

other.description: Removed deprecated gogo protocol definitions from `k8s.io/cri-api` in favor of `google.golang.org/protobuf`.
other.author: saschagrunert

enrichment.problem: Deprecated gogo protobuf definitions remained in the k8s.io/cri-api module, causing unnecessary maintenance overhead and potential incompatibility with newer protobuf tooling.
enrichment.affected: Components that import k8s.io/cri-api, such as the kubelet and CRI-compatible container runtimes, were affected by the removal of the old definitions.
enrichment.fix: Removed the old gogo protocol definitions and switched the CRI API to use the standard google.golang.org/protobuf implementation.
enrichment.impact: Simplifies the code base, reduces maintenance burden, and ensures CRI API definitions are aligned with the modern protobuf library, preventing future breakages for components that depend on cri-api.

other.description: Removed generally available feature-gate `PodDisruptionConditions`.
other.author: carlory

enrichment.problem: The GA feature‑gate `PodDisruptionConditions` was removed, which means clusters that explicitly enabled this gate will see it no longer recognized.
enrichment.affected: Users who enabled the `PodDisruptionConditions` feature‑gate in the kube‑apiserver or controller‑manager configuration.
enrichment.fix: The feature gate has been deleted because the feature is now permanently enabled (or fully removed). No action is required other than removing the gate from the configuration.
enrichment.impact: Clusters that had the gate set will need to delete the flag; the underlying pod disruption condition behavior remains unchanged for users, but any custom automation that toggles the gate will break.

other.description:
When proxying to an aggregated API server, kube-apiserver used the
`EndpointSlices` of the `service` indicated by the `APIServer`, rather than
using Endpoints.

If you were using the aggregated API server feature, and you were writing out
the endpoints for it by hand (rather than letting kube-controller-manager
generate `Endpoints` and `EndpointSlices` for it automatically based on the
Service definition), then you should write out an EndpointSlice object rather
than (or in addition to) an `Endpoints` object.
other.author: danwinship
other.userFacingChange:
When proxying to an aggregated API server, kube-apiserver now uses the
EndpointSlices of the `service` indicated by the `APIServer`, rather than
using Endpoints.

If you are using the aggregated API server feature, and you are writing out
the endpoints for it by hand (rather than letting kube-controller-manager
generate Endpoints and EndpointSlices for it automatically based on the
Service definition), then you should write out an EndpointSlice object rather
than (or in addition to) an Endpoints object.

enrichment.problem: kube-apiserver proxied requests to aggregated API servers using the legacy Endpoints objects, ignoring EndpointSlice objects. Users who manually created endpoint information for aggregated API servers (instead of relying on kube-controller-manager) could provide only EndpointSlice objects, causing the proxy to fail to route traffic.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using the aggregated API server feature with hand‑crafted endpoint resources; developers writing custom controllers or manifests for aggregated API servers.
enrichment.fix: kube-apiserver proxy logic now prefers the EndpointSlices of the Service referenced by the APIServer when forwarding traffic, falling back to Endpoints if necessary. Manual setups must create an EndpointSlice (or both EndpointSlice and Endpoints) for the aggregated API server Service.
enrichment.impact: Aggregated API server users who manually manage endpoint resources must update their manifests to include EndpointSlice objects, otherwise the aggregated API server will become unreachable. Aligns proxy behavior with the deprecation of Endpoints and supports larger endpoint sets.

other.description: kubelet:  removed the deprecated flag `--cloud-config` from the command line.
other.author: carlory

enrichment.problem: The kubelet command line flag `--cloud-config` was deprecated and has now been removed, causing kubelet startup failures for users that still specify this flag.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where the kubelet is started with the `--cloud-config` flag, typically on nodes using an external cloud provider integration.
enrichment.fix: The flag is eliminated from the kubelet binary. Users must stop passing `--cloud-config` and configure cloud provider settings via the kubelet configuration file or other supported mechanisms.
enrichment.impact: Node agents that still rely on the `--cloud-config` flag will need to update their startup scripts or configuration. Once updated, kubelet will start normally, preventing node startup errors.

other.description: Updated `conntrack` reconciler to consider a Service’s target port during cleanup of stale flow entries.
other.author: aroradaman
other.userFacingChange: Conntrack reconciler now considers service's target port during cleanup of stale flow entries.

enrichment.problem: The conntrack reconciler cleaned up stale conntrack entries without considering a Service’s targetPort, which could cause legitimate flow entries to be removed when the service port and target port differ.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes Services that use a different targetPort from the service port (e.g., NodePort, ClusterIP, LoadBalancer) could experience unexpected connection drops during conntrack cleanup.
enrichment.fix: The reconciler logic was updated to include the Service’s target port when identifying stale conntrack entries, ensuring only truly obsolete flows are removed.
enrichment.impact: Prevents accidental termination of active connections for Services that map a service port to a different targetPort, improving traffic stability and reducing connection errors.

other.description: Migrated Memory Manager to contextual logging.
other.author: swatisehgal
other.userFacingChange: Migrate Memory Manager to contextual logging

other.description: Migrated `pkg/kubelet/status` to use contextual logging.
other.author: Chulong-Li
other.userFacingChange: Migrate pkg/kubelet/status to contextual logging

enrichment.problem: The kubelet status module used unstructured logging, making it difficult to correlate log entries with specific request contexts and reducing log usefulness for debugging.

other.description: Removed an inaccurate statement about requiring ports when the Pod spec `hostNetwork` field was set.

issueContext.title: API docs for Pod `hostNetwork` mode are wrong.

> hostNetwork (boolean)

other.description: Migrated `pkg/kubelet/winstats` to contextual logging.

other.description: Masked access to Linux thermal interrupt information exposed via `/proc` and `/sys`.

other.description: Upgraded CoreDNS to v1.12.1.

other.description:
Removed "endpoint-controller" and "workload-leader-election" FlowSchemas from the default APF configuration.

migrate the lock type used in the leader election in your workloads from configmapsleases/endpointsleases to leases.
other.author: tosi3k

Removed "endpoint-controller" and "workload-leader-election" FlowSchemas from the default APF configuration.

Action required: migrate the lock type used in the leader election in your workloads from configmapsleases/endpointsleases to leases.

issueContext.title: vishvananda Netlink breaking changes in 1.2.1
issueContext.body:
The vishvananda netlink library had a behavior change in 1.2.1 , see https://github.com/vishvananda/netlink/pull/1018 for more details

> Before https://github.com/vishvananda/netlink/pull/925 (in v1.2.1), the flag was ignored and results were returned without an error. With that change, response handling is aborted, results are discarded, and unix.EINTR is returned.

We are impacted by that change https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fc7520b32f1287b867377aaee89412482199d14a/go.mod#L63 

In order to recover the previous behavior and being more resilient to partial results we should adopt a similar solution to the one adopted by moby developers, wrapping the library to retry a few times

We need to implement something like https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/48407/commits/00bf437d84ac1aec5ce24ffc5f1b7dbb6309263b#diff-28da2a9c14d97c7755152d3ad995389ceda8cc7655c8e03e2874b6d44f977ec1

We also should have some way of linting to avoid adding new netlink calls that are susceptible to get interrupted without the wrapper

/sig network
/priority important-soon

enrichment.problem: The vishvananda/netlink library changed its behavior in v1.2.1, causing EINTR errors and discarding partial results. This broke the interaction between the kubelet's CNI plugin calls and the kernel, leading to pod networking failures on nodes using older CNI plugin versions.
enrichment.affected: Nodes running the kubelet that invoke CNI plugins for pod networking; pods whose network setup could fail due to netlink interruptions.
enrichment.fix: Update the bundled CNI plugins to v1.7.1, which includes a wrapper that retries netlink calls and restores the previous tolerant behavior, preventing pod creation failures due to interrupted netlink operations.
enrichment.impact: Restores reliable pod network provisioning, reduces node‑level networking errors, and improves overall cluster stability for workloads that rely on CNI networking.

enrichment.fix: The apiserver now treats patch‑decoding failures as webhook call failures. Such failures trigger the webhook's configured failurePolicy (e.g., fail‑open or fail‑closed) and are recorded in metrics like `webhook_fail_open_count`.
enrichment.impact: Clusters using mutating admission webhooks get correct error handling and observability. Incorrect or malformed patches will now respect the intended failure policy, preventing silent acceptance of bad changes and improving debugging through accurate metrics.

issueContext.title: DRA: pod deletion delayed although NodePrepareResources was never issued
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

I am revamping our E2E tests so that they run through test cases without DRA drivers. Those tests then can become conformance tests.

Here's one scenario:
- ResourceSlices published by control plane (e.g. network-attached)
- pod scheduled
- pod startup fails (cannot call NodePrepareResources)
- delete pod
-> hangs

There is this event:
```
  Warning  FailedPrepareDynamicResources  81s   kubelet            Failed to prepare dynamic resources: failed to get gRPC client for driver dra-1411.k8s.io: plugin name dra-1411.k8s.io not found in the list of registered DRA plugins
```

It looks like the kubelet assumes that NodePrepareResources might have been called and therefore blocks pod termination while trying to call NodeUnprepareResources. 

cc @bart0sh 


### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet should track whether it really issued a `NodePrepareResources`, not just that it tried to do that. Then deleting the pod should proceed.

Rationale: if a pod lands on a node by mistake, then deleting the pod should be sufficient to recover from that mistake.

Also, the error message is a bit too verbose. The driver name should be given once, and "not found in the list" could be shortened? Also, don't repeat the word "failed". The innermost error can use it if there truly was a failure, but wrapping an error should then only add context.

```
prepare dynamic resources: get gRPC client for driver dra-1411.k8s.io: plugin not registered
```


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131956

```
dlv test ./test/e2e -- -ginkgo.focus "control plane with single node.*supports external claim referenced by multiple containers of multiple pods"  -test.v -ginkgo.v -v=3
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>

</details>


### OS version

<deta

enrichment.problem: When a pod is scheduled onto a node that does not have the required Device Resource Allocation (DRA) driver running, kubelet mistakenly assumes it has already called NodePrepareResources and blocks pod deletion while trying to call NodeUnprepareResources, causing the pod to hang on deletion.
enrichment.affected: Users running pods that require a DRA driver on nodes where the driver is absent or not registered; clusters using Dynamic Resource Allocation.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now tracks whether it actually issued a NodePrepareResources call. If the call was never made (e.g., driver not registered), kubelet no longer blocks pod termination. Error messages have also been simplified.
enrichment.impact: Pods that land on nodes without the needed DRA driver can now be deleted promptly, restoring normal cluster operation and reducing manual intervention or node restarts to recover from scheduling mistakes.

other.author: alvaroaleman
other.userFacingChange: Add a `runtime.ApplyConfiguration` interface that is implemented by all generated applyconfigs

issueContext.title: Implement common interface in applyconfigs to make them identifiable as such
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make all generated applyconfigs implement some common interface that makes them identifiable as such, similiar to `runtime.Object`. How exactly that interface looks doesn't matter, it could be a simple `IsApplyConfig() bool`.

### Why is this needed?

In order to be able to offer a good UX for SSA, dynamic clients such as controller-runtimes need a first-class `Apply` or similiar method. In order for that method to be easy to use, it needs to only accept applyconfigs. Because applyconfigs do not implement a common interface, this isn't possible today and such a method needs to accept `any`.

enrichment.problem: Generated apply configuration types did not share a common interface, so they could not be distinguished from arbitrary objects. Dynamic clients (e.g., controller-runtime) therefore had to accept `any` when exposing an Apply/SSA method, reducing type safety and UX.
enrichment.affected: Go developers using generated apply‑config structs and libraries such as controller‑runtime; code that builds apply configurations for server‑side apply.
enrichment.fix: Introduce a new `runtime.ApplyConfiguration` interface and have all generated apply configuration structs implement it. This provides a uniform marker that client libraries can require.
enrichment.impact: Developers can now write client methods that accept only apply configurations, enabling compile‑time checks and clearer APIs for server‑side apply. Improves ergonomics for controller authors and other users of dynamic clients.

other.description: Simplied validation error message for invalid fields by removing redundant field name.
other.author: xiaoweim

issueContext.title: Validation cleanups needed: proper use of "Required" and "Invalid"
issueContext.body:
Looking at validation code, I see places that are using the last argument to `field.Required` that do not need to be.  It's extra detail that is almost never needed.  For example:

```
field.Required(fldPath.Child("type"), "must specify a metric source type"))
```

This seems totally redundant - the error already says that a field named "type" is required.  It is occasionally useful to add additioninfo, such as:

```
field.Required(fldPath.Child("maxUnavailable"), "cannot be 0 when maxSurge is 0"))
```

Likewise, `field.Invalid` has details which are more often used, but the details should not repeat the field name.

Also, sometimes Invalid is used, when required would be better:

```
allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(fldPath, "", "bootstrapToken or file must be set"))
```

enrichment.problem: Validation error messages included redundant field names, causing overly verbose and confusing messages (e.g., "type is required: must specify a metric source type").
enrichment.affected: Any client or tool that receives validation errors from the Kubernetes API server (e.g., kubectl, CI pipelines, custom controllers).
enrichment.fix: The validation utilities now omit the redundant field name in `field.Required` and `field.Invalid` calls, producing concise messages that only state the issue without repeating the field name.
enrichment.impact: Users and developers get clearer, shorter error messages when submitting invalid resources, making debugging and troubleshooting faster and less error‑prone.

issueContext.body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

> Uncomment only one, leave it on its own line: 
>
/kind bug
> /kind feature


**What happened**:
It looks like validation of HPA is insufficient:
- metric name in pods and object metrics should be checked using IsValidPathSegmentName as they're used as part of request to custom metrics API (this is analogous to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/60433).

other.author: AwesomePatrol
other.userFacingChange: kubeadm: instead of passing the etcd flag --experimental-initial-corrupt-check, set the InitialCorruptCheck=true etcd feature gate, and instead of passing the --experimental-watch-progress-notify-interval flag, pass its graduated variant --watch-progress-notify-interval.

enrichment.fix: kubeadm now enables the graduated etcd feature gate InitialCorruptCheck=true and uses the stable flag --watch-progress-notify-interval instead of the experimental variants.
enrichment.impact: Ensures kubeadm continues to work after the experimental flags are removed, prevents startup failures, and aligns kubeadm with the graduated etcd feature set.

enrichment.fix: The plugin’s logging verbosity for these frequent messages was lowered from V(4) to V(5), reducing the amount of log output generated during normal scheduling operations.
enrichment.impact: Operators see fewer noisy logs from the scheduler, improving log readability and reducing storage/processing overhead for log collection systems. No functional change to scheduling behavior.

feature.description: Ensured that non-scheduling related errors (e.g., network errors) did not lengthen the Pod scheduling backoff time.
feature.author: sanposhiho
feature.userFacingChange: Non-scheduling related errors (e.g., network errors) don't lengthen the Pod scheduling backoff time.

issueContext.title: not increment pInfo.Attempts when the scheduling fails with Error status
issueContext.body:
The current `pInfo.Attempts` is simple; when the scheduler `Pop()` the pod, it increments `pInfo.Attempts`.
And, also this `pInfo.Attempts` is used to calculate the backoff time.

There are basically two failures that the scheduling cycle could make; Unschedulable or Error.
- Unschedulable: the Pod is unschedulable; e.g., no node has enough resource, nodeaffinity, etc.
- Error: the Pod cannot be scheduled because of unexpected errors;  e.g., kube-apiserver is unstable, network issue, etc.

Given [the backoff is a penalty of wasting the scheduling cycle](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8fe10dc378b7cc3b077b83aef86622e1019302d5/pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go#L205-L207), we shouldn't increment `Attempts` when the Pod comes back to queue with Error status
so that the backoff time doesn't get longer by those errors.

As the actual example, what could happen now is:
1. The scheduler fails to schedule all the pods because the cluster is under the networking issue.
2. `pInfo.Attempts` in all the Pods gets bigger and bigger meanwhile. 
3. The network issue is resolved and some Pods go scheduled.
4. But, then if some Pods fail, they have a large `pInfo.Attempts`, and hence gets super long backoff time, which is unfair because the most of their `Attempts` are failed not by the scheduling reason, but by the network issue.

/kind feature
/assign
/sig scheduling

enrichment.problem: When the scheduler encounters non‑scheduling errors (e.g., network or API‑server failures), it incorrectly increments the pod's scheduling attempt counter, causing the backoff interval to grow unnecessarily.
enrichment.affected: All Pods that experience transient scheduling errors (e.g., due to network problems) and the clusters where such errors occur.
enrichment.fix: The scheduler now skips incrementing `pInfo.Attempts` for pods that fail with an `Error` status, so only true unschedulable failures increase the backoff delay.
enrichment.impact: Pods that were blocked by transient network or API issues will be rescheduled much faster once the issue is resolved, avoiding excessively long backoff periods and improving overall cluster responsiveness.

feature.description: The Kubernetes API server merged selectors built from `matchLabelKeys` into the `labelSelector` of `topologySpreadConstraints`, aligning Pod Topology Spread behavior with Inter-Pod Affinity. To prevent breaking existing Pods using `matchLabelKeys`, this scheduler behavior was preserved until v1.34. Upgrades from v1.32 to v1.34 should be done incrementally (v1.32 → v1.33 → v1.34), ensuring Pods created at v1.32 with `matchLabelKeys` are scheduled before reaching v1.34. Controllers relying on `matchLabelKeys` no longer need to handle them directly and can use `labelSelector` instead. The new feature gate `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpreadSelectorMerge`, enabled by default, controls this behavior.
feature.author: mochizuki875
feature.userFacingChange:
Kubernetes api-server now merges selectors built from matchLabelKeys into the labelSelector of topologySpreadConstraints, 
aligning Pod Topology Spread with the approach used by Inter-Pod Affinity.

To avoid breaking existing pods that use matchLabelKeys, the current scheduler behavior will be preserved until it is removed in v1.34. 
Therefore, do not upgrade your scheduler directly from v1.32 to v1.34. 
Instead, upgrade step-by-step (from v1.32 to v1.33, then to v1.34), 
ensuring that any pods created at v1.32 with matchLabelKeys are either removed or already scheduled by the time you reach v1.34.

If you maintain controllers that previously relied on matchLabelKeys (for instance, to simulate scheduling), 
you likely no longer need to handle matchLabelKeys directly. Instead, you can just rely on the labelSelector field going forward.

Additionally, a new feature gate `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpreadSelectorMerge`, which is enabled by default, has been 
added to control this behavior.

issueContext.title: `matchLabelKeys` in PodTopologySpread should insert a labelSelector like PodAffinity's `matchLabelKeys`
issueContext.body:
follow up: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4001#discussion_r1206841191

Currently, we have matchLabelKeys in two places, PodAffinity and PodTopologySpread.
Historically, PodTopologySpread's one was introduced first and then PodAffinity.

When we designed PodAffinity, we decided to take a different approach from PodTopologySpread.
PodTopologySpread handles `matchLabelKeys` within the plugin, internally merging the label selector made from `matchLabelKeys` and calculating the result. It's not that the plugin patches an actual label selector thru kube-apiserver, but it's just that the plugin internally merges the selector with matchLabelKeys before the calculation. Therefore, if you query the pod, the pod would not has the labelSelector coming from matchLabelKeys.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3c229949f992d9f798bcfd9f79dab88c21500c36/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/common.go#L95-L106

But, PodAffinity's `matchLabelKeys` is handled at kube-apiserver; when a PodAffinity has `matchLabelKeys`, a label selector is computed from the pod's label, added additionally into `labelSelector`, and actually stored in the storage (etcd). i.e., if you query the pod after the creation, the pod would has the labelSelector that you didn't add on your own, but is made from `matchLabelKeys`. And the PodAffinity plugin doesn't directly look at `matchLabelKeys`, but just compute `labelSelector` which may or may not have the selector made from `matchLabelKeys`.

https://github.com/sanposhiho/kubernetes/blob/810e9e212ec5372d16b655f57b9231d8654a2179/pkg/registry/core/pod/strategy.go#L797-L817

We should make PodTopologySpread's `matchLabelKeys` behave the same as PodTopologySpread to reduce the users' confusion coming from the behavior difference.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature
/cc @alculquicondor @macsko @dom4ha

enrichment.problem: PodTopologySpread and PodAffinity handled `matchLabelKeys` differently: PodTopologySpread merged it internally without persisting a labelSelector, while PodAffinity created and stored a labelSelector. This inconsistency could break scheduling of existing Pods that rely on `matchLabelKeys` when the behavior changes.
enrichment.affected: Pods that use `topologySpreadConstraints` with `matchLabelKeys`, and any controllers or workloads that create such Pods. Users upgrading directly from v1.32 to v1.34 are also affected.
enrichment.fix: The API server now automatically merges selectors built from `matchLabelKeys` into the `labelSelector` field of `topologySpreadConstraints`, making PodTopologySpread behavior consistent with PodAffinity. A new feature gate `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpreadSelectorMerge` (enabled by default) controls this merging, and the scheduler continues the old behavior until v1.34 to preserve compatibility.
enrichment.impact: Controllers no longer need to generate or manage `matchLabelKeys` manually; they can rely on the `labelSelector` field. Clusters upgrading from v1.32 to v1.34 must do a stepwise upgrade (v1.32 → v1.33 → v1.34) and ensure Pods created with `matchLabelKeys` are scheduled or removed before reaching v1.34. This prevents unexpected scheduling failures after the merge removal.

feature.description: The Scheduling Framework exposed `NodeInfos` to the PreFilter plugins. The PreFilter plugins now accepted the `NodeInfo` list from the arguments.

feature.userFacingChange:
Scheduling Framework exposes NodeInfos to the PreFilterPlugins.
Action Required: The PreFilterPlugins need to accept the NodeInfo list from the arguments.

issueContext.title: Sched Framework: Request to expose NodeInfo to PreFilter plugins and Score plugins
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

In #119987 and #121954, the scheduling framework introduced `NodeInfo` as a parameter in the `RunPreScorePlugins` and `RunScorePlugins` functions of the `PluginsRunner` interface. Thank @Huang-Wei and @AxeZhan for these improvements that have made the framework easier to use. However, `NodeInfo` is still not exposed to the functions of the `ScorePlugin` and `PreFilterPlugin` interfaces (see [relevant code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go#L929)), which remains inconvenient for plugin users like [Koordinator](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator).

For instance, Koordinator aims to support [directive preemption](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220609-resource-reservation.md). To achieve this, it has had to propose [specific extensions](https://github.com/koordinator-sh/koordinator/blob/main/docs/proposals/scheduling/20220513-enhanced-scheduler-extension.md) to construct `NodeInfo` with reserved resources during the scheduling cycle.

Currently, while the `RunScorePlugins` function of the `PluginsRunner` interface accepts `NodeInfo` as a parameter, it does not pass it directly to the individual `Score` plugins. The relevant interface definitions are as follows:

```golang
type ScorePlugin interface {
	Plugin
	Score(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod, nodeName string) (int64, *Status)
	ScoreExtensions() ScoreExtensions
}

type PreFilterPlugin interface {
	Plugin
	PreFilter(ctx context.Context, state *CycleState, p *v1.Pod) (*PreFilterResult, *Status)
	PreFilterExtensions() PreFilterExtensions
}

type PluginsRunner interface {
	RunPreScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) *Status
	RunScorePlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, []*NodeInfo) ([]NodePluginScores, *Status)
	RunFilterPlugins(context.Context, *CycleState, *v1.Pod, *NodeInfo) *Status
	RunPreFilterExtens

enrichment.problem: PreFilter plugins could not access the list of NodeInfo objects, making it difficult for plugin authors (e.g., Koordinator) to implement advanced scheduling logic such as directive preemption or resource reservation.
enrichment.affected: Authors of PreFilter plugins and workloads that rely on custom scheduling behavior (e.g., Koordinator) are affected because they can now use node‑level data directly.
enrichment.fix: The scheduling framework now exposes the NodeInfo slice to PreFilter plugins via the plugin arguments, and PreFilter plugins are required to accept this NodeInfo list.
enrichment.impact: Plugin developers can now base pre‑filter decisions on full node topology and resource information, enabling richer scheduling extensions and reducing the need for custom work‑arounds.
